section.heading: 10.6. Conic Sections in Polar Coordinates
section.paragraph: In Section 10.5 we defined the parabola in terms of a focus and directrix, but we defined the ellipse and hyperbola in terms of two foci. In this section we give a more unified treatment of all three types of conic sections in terms of a focus and directrix.
section.heading: A Unified Description of Conics
section.paragraph: If we place the focus at the origin, then a conic section has a simple polar equation, which provides a convenient description of the motion of planets, satellites, and comets.

section.paragraph: When rotating conic sections, we find it much more convenient to use polar equations than Cartesian equations. We just use the fact (see Exercise 10.3.65) that the graph of $$r = f(\theta - \alpha)$$ is the graph of $$r = f(\theta)$$ rotated counterclockwise about the origin through an angle $$\alpha$$ .

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: If the ellipse of Example 2 is rotated through an angle $$\pi \slash 4$$ about the origin, find a polar equation and graph the resulting ellipse.
Solution We get the equation of the rotated ellipse by replacing $$\theta$$ with $$\theta - \pi \slash 4$$ in the equation given in Example 2. So the new equation is
$$r = \frac{10}{3 - 2\cos(\theta - \pi \slash 4)}$$
We use this equation to graph the rotated ellipse in Figure 5. Notice that the ellipse has been rotated about its left focus.

section.heading: Kepler’s Laws
section.paragraph: In 1609 the German mathematician and astronomer Johannes Kepler, on the basis of huge amounts of astronomical data, published the following three laws of planetary motion.

list.item: A planet revolves around the sun in an elliptical orbit with the sun at one focus.
The line joining the sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
The square of the period of revolution of a planet is proportional to the cube of the length of the major axis of its orbit.

section.paragraph: Although Kepler formulated his laws in terms of the motion of planets around the sun, they apply equally well to the motion of moons, comets, satellites, and other bodies that orbit subject to a single gravitational force. In Section 13.4 we will show how to deduce Kepler’s Laws from Newton’s Laws. Here we use Kepler’s First Law, together with the polar equation of an ellipse, to calculate quantities of interest in astronomy.

For purposes of astronomical calculations, it’s useful to express the equation of an ellipse in terms of its eccentricity $$e$$ and its semimajor axis $$a$$ . We can write the distance $$d$$ from the focus to the directrix in terms of $$a$$ if we use (4):
So $$ed = a(1 - e^{2})$$ . If the directrix is $$x = d$$ , then the polar equation is
The polar equation of an ellipse with focus at the origin, semimajor axis $$a$$ , eccentricity $$e$$ , and directrix $$x = d$$ can be written in the form

The positions of a planet that are closest to and farthest from the sun are called its perihelion and aphelion, respectively, and correspond to the vertices of the ellipse (see Figure 7). The distances from the sun to the perihelion and aphelion are called the perihelion distance and aphelion distance, respectively. In Figure 1 the sun is at the focus $$F$$ , so at perihelion we have $$\theta = 0$$ and, from Equation 7,
$$r = \frac{a\left( 1 - e^{2} \right)}{1 + e\cos 0} = \frac{a(1 - e)(1 + e)}{1 + e} = a(1 - e)$$
Similarly, at aphelion $$\theta = \pi$$ and $$r = a(1 + e)$$ .

The left and right-most points on the ellipse are labeled aphelion and perihelion, respectively, and are connected by a line segment. The right focus of the ellipse, which lies on the line segment, is labeled sun. From the point labeled sun, another line segment, labeled r, slopes upward to the left, at an angle theta from the first line segment, and meets the ellipse at a point labeled planet.

section.paragraph: The perihelion distance from a planet to the sun is $$a(1 - e)$$ and the aphelion distance is $$a(1 + e)$$ .

example.heading: Example 5

list.item: (a) Find an approximate polar equation for the elliptical orbit of the earth around the sun (at one focus) given that the eccentricity is about $$0.017$$ and the length of the major axis is about $$2.99 \times 10^{8}$$ km.
(b) Find the distance from the earth to the sun at perihelion and at aphelion.

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) The length of the major axis is $$2a = 2.99 \times 10^{8}$$ , so $$a = 1.495 \times 10^{8}$$ . We are given that $$e = 0.017$$ and so, from Equation 7, an equation of the earth’s orbit around the sun is $$r = \frac{a(1 - e^{2})}{1 + e\cos\theta} = \frac{(1.495 \times 10^{8})\lbrack 1 - \left. (0.017 \right)^{2}\rbrack}{1 + 0.017\cos\theta}$$ or, approximately, $$r = \frac{1.49 \times 10^{8}}{1 + 0.017\cos\theta}$$

(b) From (8), the perihelion distance from the earth to the sun is $$a(1 - e) \approx (1.495 \times 10^{8})(1 - 0.017) \approx 1.47 \times 10^{8}{km}$$ and the aphelion distance is $$a(1 + e) \approx (1.495 \times 10^{8})(1 + 0.017) \approx 1.52 \times 10^{8}{km}$$
